summary: HNCP is an extensible configuration protocol for home networks, built as a profile of DNCP. It lets routers discover network borders and automatically configure addressing, routing, naming and service discovery, and it sets out requirements for home network devices.

plainLanguage.summary: HNCP is a protocol that lets the routers in a home network share what they know, so the network configures itself. They work out where the network border is, split up the address space the providers give them, and agree on which router provides each service.

questions: how does hncp find the network border
how do home routers assign prefixes automatically
subtitle: How home routers share state so a multi-router, multi-ISP home network configures itself.

tldr.problem: A home network with several routers and more than one internet provider has to work out which addresses, routes, names and services belong where, and do it without the user configuring anything.
tldr.mechanism: HNCP is a profile of DNCP: the routers exchange state as TLVs over UDP port 8231, agree on prefixes with a common assignment algorithm, and elect one router for each service on each link.
tldr.outcome: Addressing, routing, name resolution and service discovery in the home become automatic. RFC 7788 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 8375.

today: RFC 7788 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2016. It was later updated by RFC 8375, which reserved the home.arpa. domain for home networks, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What HNCP Is For
sections.content:
The Home Networking Control Protocol is designed to let home routers share state, to serve the needs of the IPv6 home network architecture in RFC 7368. That architecture assumes zero-configuration operation, several subnets, several home routers, and possibly several upstream service providers each giving the home network one or more prefixes. RFC 7368 sets no requirements for IPv4, but HNCP is designed with dual-stack operation in mind.

The shared state is carried as type-length-value objects in the DNCP node state, and it enables:

  • Automatic discovery of the network border, based on the DNCP topology.
  • Automatic division of the prefixes the providers delegate, and assignment of prefixes to both HNCP and non-HNCP routers, using the algorithm in RFC 7695. Assigned prefixes give addresses to devices that are not HNCP aware, using stateless address autoconfiguration and DHCP, and give HNCP nodes space to pick their own addresses from.
  • Internal and external name resolution, and service discovery across several links.
  • Other services not defined in the document that need state shared between home nodes and do not change rapidly.

Because HNCP uses DNCP as its state synchronisation protocol, the DNCP applicability statement applies: it should not carry data that changes rapidly and constantly. Where such data has to be published, a more suitable protocol should carry it and HNCP should only announce where to find that server. Naming and service discovery are an example: HNCP carries DNS server addresses, not per-name or per-service host data.

HNCP is link-layer agnostic. It works on any link that supports IPv6 link-local multicast and unicast, and its trickle retransmissions and keep-alives handle packet loss and links that are not transitively connected, so the network converges eventually. It is meant for routers, but advanced hosts can use it too.
sections.plainLanguage: HNCP is for homes with more than one router and more than one internet provider. The routers tell each other what they know, and the network works out addresses, routes and names by itself. It does not carry data that changes all the time, so it is not a substitute for a normal service protocol.

sections.title: The DNCP Profile
sections.content:
HNCP is a profile of the Distributed Node Consensus Protocol in RFC 7787, and it defines the transport and synchronisation details for sharing state between nodes.

  • Transport. HNCP uses UDP datagrams on port 8231 over link-local scoped IPv6, with unicast and multicast. The HNCP group address is FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:11. A received datagram whose source or destination address is not link-local scoped MUST be ignored, and a reply to a multicast or unicast message MUST go back to the source address and port of the original message. Each node MUST be able to receive, and potentially reassemble, UDP datagrams with a payload of at least 4000 bytes.
  • Identifiers. HNCP runs only on multicast-capable interfaces, and each node MUST assign a non-zero 32-bit endpoint identifier to every interface where HNCP is enabled. Those identifiers MUST be unique within the node, and using values equivalent to the IPv6 link-local scope identifiers is RECOMMENDED. Node identifiers are opaque 32-bit values and a node SHOULD use a random one; if a collision happens, the node MUST immediately generate and use a new random identifier that no other node is using.
  • Hashing. HNCP nodes MUST use the leading 64 bits of the MD5 message digest as the DNCP hash function H(x) used to build the DNCP hash tree.
  • Keep-alives. The per-endpoint keep-alive extension is used on all endpoints. The suggested default interval is 20 seconds. The suggested multiplier is 2.1 on a virtually lossless link, which allows for one lost keep-alive, and a considerably higher multiplier such as 15 on a lossy link.
  • Trickle. For each per-interface Trickle instance, k SHOULD be 1, so the timer resets when data is updated and retransmissions handle loss. Imin SHOULD be 200 milliseconds and MUST NOT be lower, and Imax SHOULD be 7 doublings of Imin and MUST NOT be lower.
  • Security. Unicast traffic SHOULD be secured with DTLS as described in DNCP when it crosses an unsecured link, using UDP port 8232. A node implementing HNCP security MUST support the DNCP Pre-Shared Key method, SHOULD support the PKI-based trust method, and MAY support the certificate-based trust consensus method.
  • Multicast integrity. HNCP nodes MUST ignore all Node-State TLVs received via multicast on a link where DNCP security is enabled, so that node state changes cannot be spoofed.
sections.plainLanguage: The routers talk to each other over UDP port 8231, using IPv6 addresses that only work on the local link, and they meet at a fixed multicast address. Unicast messages can be protected with DTLS on port 8232, and multicast state updates are ignored on secured links so they cannot be forged.

sections.title: Interface Classification and Border Discovery
sections.content:
Each interface is put in a category, and the categories decide how the node treats it. Internal means the interface is inside the borders of the HNCP network; it MUST operate as a DNCP endpoint, and every node must implement this category, which is also the default. External means the interface is outside the borders; it MUST NOT operate as a DNCP endpoint, and HNCP routers MUST implement this category. Leaf is for client devices only: it is internal, except that it MUST NOT operate as a DNCP endpoint. Guest is for untrusted client devices; in addition to the Leaf restrictions, the router MUST filter traffic so that those devices cannot reach other devices inside the network or query their advertised services unless explicitly allowed. Ad Hoc is internal but makes no assumption that the link is transitively connected. Hybrid is internal while still trying to acquire external configuration on that link, for example by running DHCP clients, which suits a link shared with a non-HNCP router inside the same network.

Auto-detection is possible from the behaviour of DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 prefix delegation servers on the connected link. To tell its own servers apart from external ones, all internal devices running DHCP servers on links where auto-detection is used MUST ignore or reject DHCP requests carrying a DHCP user class consisting of the ASCII string "HOMENET". Not following this rule can cause false positives, where a node treats an intended internal interface as external.

The classification algorithm stops at the first match. If a fixed category is configured for an interface, that is used. Otherwise, if a delegated prefix could be acquired by running a DHCPv6 client, the interface is external, and if an IPv4 address could be acquired by running a DHCPv4 client, the interface is external. In both cases the client MUST have included the "HOMENET" user class in all of its requests. Otherwise the interface is considered internal. Because other HNCP nodes ignore a client with that user class, any server that does reply is clearly external, or a malicious internal node.

The border is then defined implicitly: every interface that is not in the External category is inside the borders, and every other one is outside. A router using auto-detection MUST run the DHCP clients as long as the interface is active, and rerun the algorithm so that it reacts to a change of category. It SHOULD wait a reasonable time, 5 seconds by default, for the clients to obtain a lease before treating a newly activated or previously external interface as internal.
sections.plainLanguage: Each port is labelled internal or external, and the external ones are the network border. The label can be set by hand or worked out automatically: the router asks for an address with DHCP, and if an outside server answers, the port is external. Internal servers ignore requests carrying the user class HOMENET, so they never answer.

sections.title: Prefix Assignment
sections.content:
Border routers first share what they learned from the service providers or from local configuration, publishing one External-Connection TLV per external connection. Those containers hold Delegated-Prefix TLVs, and the prefix assignment algorithm in RFC 7695 then hands prefixes to the internal links.

The algorithm's parameters are fixed for HNCP. Node identifiers are the HNCP node identifiers, compared bitwise. The set of delegated prefixes is the set of prefixes in Delegated-Prefix TLVs that are not strictly included in prefixes in other Delegated-Prefix TLVs. The set of shared links is the set of Common Links belonging to interfaces in the Internal, Leaf, Guest or Ad Hoc category. Private Links represent DHCPv6 prefix delegation clients, and prefixes in the DHCPv6 Exclude Prefix option. The set of advertised prefixes is what other nodes publish in Assigned-Prefix TLVs.

Several timing parameters are given. ADOPT_MAX_DELAY defaults to 0 seconds, so prefix adoption is instant. BACKOFF_MAX_DELAY defaults to 4 seconds, RANDOM_SET_SIZE defaults to 64, and the flooding delay defaults to 5 seconds. The default advertised prefix priority is 2.

A new prefix is only assigned when the rules allow it. If a Delegated-Prefix TLV carries a DHCPv6-Data TLV and the node does not understand one of the DHCP options in it, no new prefix is created. If the remaining preferred lifetime of the prefix is 0 and another delegated prefix of the same IP version with a non-zero preferred lifetime is in use, no new prefix is created. Otherwise a new prefix is desired, unless the Delegated-Prefix TLV carries a Prefix-Policy TLV of type 131 that restricts assignment and no local policy allows it anyway.

For an IPv6 delegated prefix, a prefix of length 64 MUST be selected whenever at least one of that length is available, unless configured otherwise; a longer prefix MAY be selected if no length 64 prefix is available. For an IPv4 delegated prefix, a prefix of length 24 SHOULD be preferred. When a router makes an assignment, it MUST support a way to hand out addresses from that prefix if the link is for clients, which means announcing the L-capability for IPv4 and the H-capability for an IPv6 prefix longer than 64.

Once a prefix is applied to a Common Link, every router on that link MUST forward traffic for it to that link, MUST take part in the client configuration election, and MAY add an address from it to the interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router receives address space from its provider and publishes it to the others. A shared algorithm then hands out one piece to each internal link, so two routers on the same link do not hand out the same addresses. IPv6 links normally get a 64-bit prefix, IPv4 links a 24-bit one.

sections.title: Configuring Hosts and Non-HNCP Routers
sections.content:
HNCP routers must make sure that hosts and downstream routers that do not speak HNCP get addresses and routes. Since a DHCP client usually binds to one server at a time, an election takes place for each link and each service.

For IPv6, stateless address autoconfiguration in RFC 4861 is the normal way to configure clients, because of its low overhead and fast renumbering. Each router therefore sends Router Advertisements on interfaces meant for clients, and MUST include a Prefix Information Option for each applied assigned prefix that it assigned to that link. Stateful DHCPv6 can be added by administrative choice, for example to collect hostnames for naming services or where stateless configuration does not apply.

Four elections happen on a Common Link, and all of them use the same rule: the router that advertises the greatest capability value for that service wins. If there is a tie, the routers' combined capability values are compared, and if there is still a tie, the router with the greatest node identifier wins.

  • The stateful DHCPv6 server is elected by the H-capability. The winner MUST serve stateful DHCPv6, and SHOULD provide naming services for the hostnames it acquires. All other nodes MUST NOT serve stateful DHCPv6. Leases SHOULD be assigned in a way that does not hinder fast renumbering, for example by handing out addresses only from locally generated prefixes and from prefixes whose length is not 64, and by using renew and rebind times no longer than 5 minutes. If no router was elected, stateful DHCPv6 is not provided.
  • The DHCPv6 prefix delegation server is elected by the P-capability. The winner MUST provide prefix delegation on that link, and all other nodes MUST NOT.
  • The DHCPv4 server is elected by the L-capability. The winner MUST provide DHCPv4 services on the link and MUST announce itself as the router to clients. Its renew and rebind times SHOULD be no longer than 5 minutes, so that changes take effect quickly.
  • The multicast DNS proxy is elected by the M-capability. The winner MUST provide an mDNS proxy on the link.

Routers that stop being elected SHOULD invalidate the remaining bindings, where that applies, so that clients reconfigure.
sections.plainLanguage: Several routers sit on the same home link, but a client can only use one DHCP server. Each router advertises how good it is at a job, and the best one for that job takes the job. The same happens for the DNS proxy and for handing out prefixes to other routers.

sections.title: Naming and Service Discovery
sections.content:
Each HNCP router SHOULD provide and advertise a recursive name resolving server to clients that honour the announcements made in DNS-Delegated-Zone, Domain-Name and Node-Name TLVs, delegating queries to the designated name servers and handing out A, AAAA and PTR records as those TLVs describe.

Each router SHOULD also provide a name for each internal Common Link where it is the designated DHCPv4 server, stateful DHCPv6 server or mDNS proxy, or where it provides forward or reverse DNS services for connected devices. Those names are announced in DNS-Delegated-Zone TLVs and MUST be unique in the whole network. On a conflict, the announcement of the node with the greatest node identifier wins and the others MUST stop announcing it. A router providing recursive name resolving MUST use the DNS server address in the TLV to resolve names in that zone as if there were an NS record.

Each HNCP node SHOULD announce a node name for itself, and MAY announce names for other devices, using Node-Name TLVs. Those names MUST also be unique in the network, with the same rule for conflicts, and the recursive resolver MUST resolve them to their addresses as if there were A or AAAA records.

Names and unqualified zones in an HNCP network are local to that network. A network-wide zone is appended to every single label or unqualified zone to qualify it. The default is ".home", but an administrator MAY configure a different one with a Domain-Name TLV, and where several are announced, the domain of the node with the greatest node identifier takes precedence.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router gives a name to the link it serves and to itself, and publishes those names so the other routers can answer name lookups. Every short name is qualified with the network domain, which is .home unless an administrator picks something else.

sections.title: The TLVs
sections.content:
HNCP defines a set of TLVs in addition to those of DNCP. The same encoding rules and defaults apply as in Section 7 of RFC 7787, and most variable-length HNCP TLVs can carry nested TLVs, which are encoded after the variable-length content and followed by zero padding to the next 32-bit boundary. A TLV is only valid in its designated context, and one found outside that context MUST be ignored. TLVs that carry addresses or prefixes handle both address families: IPv6 information is encoded as it is, while IPv4 uses the IPv4-mapped IPv6 address format, with the prefix length increased by 96.

The HNCP-Version TLV, type 32, states the supported version and the router capabilities. Its M, P, H and L capability values are priority values for the on-link mDNS proxy, the DHCPv6 prefix delegation server, the stateful DHCPv6 server and the DHCPv4 server. Each MUST be 0 if the router cannot do that job, SHOULD be 4 otherwise, and MAY be any value from 1 to 7 for a non-default priority. The values 8 to 15 are reserved. A human-readable UTF-8 user-agent string names the implementation.

The External-Connection TLV, type 33, gathers the configuration for one external connection, and a node MAY publish any number of them. Inside it, the Delegated-Prefix TLV, type 34, advertises prefixes allocated to the whole network, with a valid lifetime, a preferred lifetime, the prefix length and the prefix itself. Its prefixes MUST NOT overlap with those of other Delegated-Prefix TLVs in the same container. The Prefix-Policy TLV, type 43, records what a delegated prefix is for: type 0 means Internet connectivity, types 1 to 128 give an explicit destination prefix, 129 a DNS domain, 130 an opaque UTF-8 string, and 131 a restrictive assignment.

The DHCPv6-Data TLV, type 37, and the DHCPv4-Data TLV, type 38, carry streams of DHCP options, for example recursive DNS server addresses. The Assigned-Prefix TLV, type 35, announces the prefixes a node has published, with the endpoint identifier, a priority from 0 to 15 and the prefix. The Node-Address TLV, type 36, announces an address a node has taken for itself. The DNS-Delegated-Zone TLV, type 39, announces a forward or reverse DNS zone delegation. The Domain-Name TLV, type 40, sets the network's base domain. The Node-Name TLV, type 41, ties a name to an address. The Managed-PSK TLV, type 42, announces a random 256-bit pre-shared key.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything the routers share is a typed object: a version and capability record, the upstream connections, the prefixes, the addresses, the names and a shared key. Each object has a number between 32 and 43 that says what it is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
HNCP enables self-configuring networks with as little user intervention as possible. That goal usually conflicts with security goals and introduces a number of threats. The general security issues of home networks are discussed in RFC 7368, and the protocols that set up addresses and routes in such networks rarely have security inside the configuration protocol itself, though those issues are out of scope for HNCP itself.

HNCP carries several kinds of information with different threat potential: network topology information such as the nodes and their common links, address assignment information such as delegated and assigned prefixes, and naming and service discovery information such as the names of links and nodes.

Interface classification brings its own threats. Because external routers do not take part in the protocol and often cannot be authenticated by other means, encrypting or authenticating HNCP traffic does not protect against them. The threats include a forged uplink in the home network, used to redirect traffic bound for outside, and forged internal status from an external router, used to get around the perimeter firewall. It is therefore imperative either to secure individual links at the physical or link layer, or to preconfigure the adjacent interfaces of HNCP routers to a fixed category, so that the home border is secure. Eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks on external traffic can still happen between the border router and the provider, but those cannot be addressed from inside the home network. DHCPv4 has defined a way to authenticate its messages in RFC 3118, but it is rarely implemented in large or small networks.

Once the border is established, there are ways to secure HNCP against internal threats such as manipulation or eavesdropping by a compromised device on a link where HNCP runs. If left unsecured, attackers can redirect traffic arbitrarily, eavesdrop, spoof, or deny service to the HNCP services, including the protocols that use HNCP-derived keys. Detailed interface categories such as Leaf and Guest help, by keeping untrusted devices out of HNCP traffic and stopping them reaching internal resources. Where that is not practical and the lower layers do not protect the link well enough, DTLS-based secure unicast transport MUST be used.

Other protocols run alongside HNCP, such as interior gateway protocols, and their own security aspects apply. Most of them support only pre-shared key authentication natively and no encryption, which affects how much an encryption-based mechanism in HNCP can help, since the home routing information is usually not encrypted anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: A network that configures itself can be misconfigured by someone who should not be able to. The document's advice is to set the internal and external ports by hand where the border matters, to keep untrusted devices off the HNCP traffic, and to use DTLS on the links that need protection.

layers.label: Home services
layers.detail: Addresses, names and services that hosts and devices use.

layers.label: HNCP
layers.detail: Shares state between home routers as TLVs, and defines the address and election rules.

layers.label: DNCP
layers.detail: Keeps the node state of the routers in agreement with each other.

layers.label: UDP port 8231
layers.detail: Multicast and unicast over IPv6 link-local, with the group address FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:11.

layers.label: DTLS port 8232
layers.detail: Optional protection for unicast traffic, as described in DNCP.

items.title: Adopt delay
items.text: ADOPT_MAX_DELAY defaults to 0 seconds, so prefix adoption is instant.

items.title: Flooding delay
items.text: The flooding delay defaults to 5 seconds.

items.title: Default priority
items.text: The default advertised prefix priority is 2.

items.title: Prefix lengths
items.text: A 64-bit prefix is used for IPv6 when one is available, and a 24-bit prefix is preferred for IPv4.

viz.caption: THE HNCP TLV TYPES (RFC 7788, SECTIONS 10 AND 13)

items.label: HNCP-Version
items.desc: Supported version, capability values and user-agent string.

items.label: External-Connection
items.desc: Container for the configuration of one upstream connection.

items.label: Delegated-Prefix
items.desc: A prefix allocated to the whole network, with its lifetimes.

items.label: Assigned-Prefix
items.desc: A prefix a node has published, with its priority.

items.label: Node-Address
items.desc: An address a node has taken for itself.

items.label: DNS-Delegated-Zone
items.desc: A forward or reverse DNS zone delegation.

items.label: Domain-Name
items.desc: The base domain name for the network.

items.label: Node-Name
items.desc: The name of a node, tied to an address.

items.label: Prefix-Policy
items.desc: What a delegated prefix is for, such as Internet connectivity.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved for future use. Must be 0 when creating the TLV and ignored when processing it.

fields.name: M, P, H and L
fields.desc: Four capability values, one four-bit priority each, for the mDNS proxy, DHCPv6-PD, stateful DHCPv6 and DHCPv4 servers. A user-agent string follows.
